title: Appendix - Build It Yourself / For Maintainers
subtitle: How the release packages are made: building the engines, packaging per platform, and (optionally) code-signing. More technical than the rest of this guide.
in_this_chapter: The pieces and where they live
Step 2 - Package the app for a platform
Step 3 - Code signing (optional, per operating system)
The one rule: sign each OS on its own machine

callout.label: IN A NUTSHELL
callout.text: From a clone of the public repo: run  build-engines  to compile VOACAP + NEC2++ into  third_party/<rid>/ , then run  package  to publish the self-contained app, bundle those engines and the license notices, and produce a ready-to-ship archive in  dist/ . Signing is optional and off by default. Do each OS's build on that OS.

blocks.p: Everyone else can ignore this - the normal way to install is to download a ready-made release and run the setup. This appendix is for a maintainer (or a technical user on a platform without a prebuilt release, such as Raspberry Pi) who wants to **produce** a distributable, or add the helper engines to a sample-mode install. The project is open source, so anyone can do this from the public source at **https://github.com/KE4CON/ActivationPlanner**.

blocks.h1: The Pieces and Where They Live

rows: Clones and builds voacapl + necpp into third_party/<rid>/ (macOS/Linux, and Windows via MSYS2).
Windows helper that runs build-engines.sh under an MSYS2 bash.
Windows: publishes self-contained, bundles engines + licenses, signs (optional), zips to dist/.
macOS/Linux: publishes self-contained, bundles engines + licenses, signs (optional), tars to dist/.
Optional Authenticode signing (Azure Trusted Signing or Key Vault). Off unless configured.
Optional Developer ID signing + notarization. Off unless configured.
The exact per-RID layout the engines must be staged into.
The notices bundled into every build (VOACAP disclaimer, NEC2++ GPLv2 + source offer).

blocks.p: "RID" is a .NET Runtime Identifier - the platform tag, such as  win-x64 ,  osx-arm64 ,  linux-x64 ,  linux-arm64 .
The engines are compiled from their public sources into the staging area. Run this on the target operating system (they're native programs):

bullets: **macOS / Linux / Raspberry Pi:**  build/build-engines.sh   (auto-detects the RID; pass one to override, e.g.  build/build-engines.sh linux-arm64 ). Run  build/build-engines.sh --check  first to verify you have git, make, gcc/g++, gfortran, and autotools.
**Windows:**  build/build-engines.ps1   (needs MSYS2 with the gcc/gfortran toolchain; the script prints the exact  pacman  packages if they're missing).

blocks.p: This stages  third_party/<rid>/voacap/{voacapl, itshfbc/}  and  third_party/<rid>/nec/nec2++ , and copies NEC2++'s GPLv2  COPYING  and a source snapshot into  licenses/nec2++/ .

callout.label: WINDOWS RUNTIME DLLs
callout.text: Engines built under MSYS2/Cygwin need their runtime DLLs (gcc/gfortran runtime, or cygwin1.dll) beside the .exe to run on a machine without MSYS2. Copy those DLLs into third_party/win-x64/voacap and .../nec after building, or build a static/native variant.

blocks.h1: Step 2 - Package the App for a Platform

blocks.p: Packaging publishes the app self-contained (no separate .NET needed by the user), bundles whatever engines are staged, copies the license notices, and produces an archive in  dist/ :

bullets: **Windows:**  build/package.ps1 -Version 1.0.0   (add  -Rid win-arm64  for ARM). Produces  dist/ActivationPlanner-1.0.0-win-x64.zip .
**macOS / Linux:**  build/package.sh <rid> 1.0.0  , e.g.  build/package.sh osx-arm64 1.0.0  or  build/package.sh linux-x64 1.0.0 . Produces a  .tar.gz  in  dist/ .

blocks.p: If the engines aren't staged, packaging still succeeds and warns - the resulting build runs in sample mode. That's the same archive an end user downloads and installs with  install.ps1 / install.sh .

blocks.h1: Step 3 - Code Signing (Optional, Per Operating System)

blocks.p: Signing is **off by default** and credential-gated, so the same pipeline makes signed or unsigned builds. Nothing in the scripts stores certificates or passwords.

bullets: **Windows, on your machine:**  package.ps1  calls  sign-windows.ps1 , which delegates to a single shared signer (default  C:\Dev\Signing and Distribution\azure\sign.ps1 , or  $env:SIGN_SCRIPT ). That script uses Azure Trusted Signing via the  sign  tool with  az login  auth. So: run  az login  once, then  package.ps1  produces a signed build; if you're not logged in (or the shared signer is absent) it skips cleanly and ships unsigned. A signed Windows build avoids the SmartScreen "unknown publisher" warning.

**Windows, in CI (GitHub Actions):** the  release.yml  workflow signs with  azure/trusted-signing-action , reading config from repo/account **variables** ( AZURE_SIGNING_ENDPOINT ,  AZURE_SIGNING_ACCOUNT ,  AZURE_SIGNING_CERT_PROFILE ) and **secrets** ( AZURE_TENANT_ID ,  AZURE_CLIENT_ID ,  AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET ). The sign step self-gates on  AZURE_SIGNING_ACCOUNT , so it's dormant until those are set. Set them once at the **account level** and every repo inherits them.

**macOS** (from  package.sh , which calls  sign-macos.sh ): set  ACTIVATIONPLANNER_SIGN=developerid  and  APPLE_SIGN_IDENTITY , plus notarization credentials. macOS signing must run **on a Mac** (codesign/notarytool are Apple-only). Not set up yet - macOS ships unsigned with the Gatekeeper fallback.

callout.label: SIGNING STATUS
callout.text: Code signing is intended but may not be operational yet. Until it is, releases ship unsigned and users follow the get-past-the-warning steps in the Windows/macOS chapters. The scripts already support signing so builds become signed the moment credentials are configured.

blocks.p: The whole matrix is supported: Windows / macOS / Linux, each on x64 or ARM. The app cross-publishes to any RID, but the **engines must be compiled on the target architecture** - so for a Raspberry Pi, build on the Pi:

steps: On a Raspberry Pi (64-bit Pi OS, Pi 4 or Pi 5 recommended):  build/build-engines.sh linux-arm64  .
Then  build/package.sh linux-arm64 1.0.0  to produce the Pi distributable.
Install it with  install.sh  as in the Linux chapter.

blocks.p: Apple Silicon uses  osx-arm64  (built on an Apple Silicon Mac); ARM Windows uses  win-arm64 .

NEC2++ is GPLv2. The build stages its  COPYING  and a source snapshot into  licenses/nec2++/ , and the packaging step bundles the whole  licenses/  folder into every build - so each distributable carries the GPLv2 text and the corresponding source (or the written offer in  NEC2++-Source-Offer.txt ). Keep this intact; it's how the redistribution stays compliant. Full detail is in  docs/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md .

blocks.h1: The One Rule: Sign Each OS on Its Own Machine

callout.label: WHERE EACH BUILD HAPPENS
callout.text: You can cross-BUILD the app for any platform from one machine, but you must SIGN each platform's build on that platform: Windows signing (Azure) runs on Windows; macOS signing + notarization (codesign/notarytool) runs only on a Mac. And because the engines are native, compile them on the target OS/architecture too. In practice: build + sign the Windows release on Windows, and the macOS release on a Mac.
